title: “You become free, you can tell her anything”: Perceptions of a peer-based medication delivery implementation strategy to improve hypertension medication adherence in western Kenya
content:
by Caroline Watiri, Juddy Wachira, Benson Njuguna, Jessica Gjonaj, Kibet Kangogo, Mercy Korir, Jeremiah Laktabai, Imran Manji, Sonak D. Pastakia, Dan N. Tran, Rajesh Vedanthan

Medication adherence is a critical component of improving hypertension-related cardiovascular disease outcomes. Challenges with access to and possession of medication contribute to poor adherence. To address these challenges, we aim to implement a strategy in rural western Kenya that combines peer delivery of medications and health information technology. We sought to assess stakeholder perceptions of the planned implementation strategy, recognizing the importance of these perceptions to optimize successful implementation. Focus group discussions were conducted among people living with hypertension, community members, and health workers. In addition, key informant interviews were conducted with public sector health administrators.. Deductive codes were generated based on a priori themes, including perceptions of peers being involved in health service provision, medication delivery, psychosocial support, and the use of health information technology. The investigator team pooled codes according to conceptual alignment and integrated them into common themes after joint review and discussion. NVIVO 12 was used for data analysis. The Peers and Technology for Adherence, Access, Accountability, and Analytics (PT4A) implementation strategy was perceived to have both benefits and potential challenges. Major themes included the importance of trust resulting from a safe space to share experiences with peers, increased access to medications, improved hypertension management at the facility and community levels, and anticipated improved health outcomes for people living with hypertension. The success of the program was felt to rely heavily on the peers’ competency and how well they communicated, which was viewed as a potential challenge by some stakeholders. This study was able to identify key perceptions regarding an implementation strategy that combines peer medication delivery and health information technology to improve hypertension medication adherence. Pre-implementation stakeholder engagement can unearth unique perspectives around perceived benefits and challenges that can be used to refine strategies to increase implementation success of evidence-based interventions in new contexts. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier (NCT number): NCT05051124.
